title: Λύκος καὶ λέων
part: The Wolf and the Lion (Chambry 227 · Perry 347)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 227 (= Perry 347). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », [ ] for words Chambry deletes as interpolated). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Λύκος ποτὲ ἄρας πρόβατον ἐκ ποίμνης ἐκόμιζεν εἰς κοίτην.
sentences.tr: Lykos pote aras probaton ek poimnēs ekomizen eis koitēn.
sentences.l: A wolf, having once carried off a sheep from a flock, was bringing it to his lair.
sentences.n: ἄρας is the aorist participle of αἴρω, 'having lifted, having taken up.' The participle for the step and the imperfect ἐκόμιζεν for the journey still under way is the ordinary engine of these fables — something always interrupts the imperfect.

sentences.t: Λέων δὲ αὐτῷ συναντήσας ἀφεῖλε τὸ πρόβατον.
sentences.tr: Leōn de autōi synantēsas apheile to probaton.
sentences.l: But a lion, having met him, took away the sheep.
sentences.n: συναντάω takes the dative of the person met. ἀφεῖλε is the active aorist of ἀφαιρέω, plain 'took away'; the wolf answers with the middle of the same verb in the next sentence, ἀφείλου.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ πόρρωθεν σταθεὶς εἶπεν· « Ἀδίκως ἀφείλου τὸ ἐμόν. »
sentences.tr: Ho de porrōthen statheis eipen· « Adikōs apheilou to emon. »
sentences.l: And he, having taken his stand at a distance, said: « Unjustly you took away what is mine. »
sentences.i: And the wolf, taking his stand well off, said: « You have taken what is mine, and unjustly. »
sentences.n: σταθείς is the aorist passive of ἵστημι used intransitively, 'took up his position' — the same pattern as στραφείς, 'turned round.' πόρρωθεν does the fable's work quietly: the wolf argues justice from a safe distance. ἀφείλου is the middle, 'you took away for yourself,' the regular voice for stripping a thing from its owner.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ λέων γελάσας ἔφη· « Σοὶ γὰρ δικαίως ὑπὸ φίλου ἐδόθη ; »
sentences.tr: Ho de leōn gelasas ephē· « Soi gar dikaiōs hypo philou edothē ; »
sentences.l: And the lion, laughing, said: « Why, was it justly given to you by a friend? »
sentences.n: γάρ in a question makes it a retort: it picks up the other speaker's word (ἀδίκως / δικαίως) and turns it back on him. ἐδόθη is the aorist passive of δίδωμι, with ὑπό and the genitive for the giver. The lion does not deny the injustice; he asks how the wolf came by the sheep.

sentences.t: [Ὅτι] ἅρπαγας καὶ πλεονέκτας λῃστὰς ἔν τινι πταίσματι κειμένους καὶ ἀλλήλους μεμφομένους ὁ μῦθος ἐλέγχει.
sentences.tr: [Hoti] harpagas kai pleonektas lēistas en tini ptaismati keimenous kai allēlous memphomenous ho mythos elenchei.
sentences.l: [That] the fable exposes rapacious and grasping robbers, lying in some mishap and blaming one another.
sentences.i: The fable exposes rapacious and grasping robbers, caught in some mishap and blaming one another.
sentences.n: Chambry prints Ὅτι in square brackets, his mark for a word he judges to have crept in later and would delete. Because he deletes the subordinator, the idiomatic line does not supply the 'the story shows' that an unbracketed bare Ὅτι would take: what is left already stands on its own with its own finite verb, ἐλέγχει. πταῖσμα is a stumble, and so a fall into trouble; κειμένους is to be lying there in it. ἐλέγχω is to put a man to the proof and so show him up.
